                                   Introduction

         The influence of emerging technologies on language education has
long been explored, but the advent of large language model (LLM)-powered
Artificial Intelligence (AI) represents a significant shift, accelerating changes
in language teaching and learning. Recent studies highlight the instructional
potential of tools like ChatGPT (e.g., Hockly, 2023; Kasneci et al., 2023;
Kohnke et al., 2023), but also identifying challenges for English language
education. Kasneci et al. (2023) outline both the benefits, such as enhanced
reading, writing, and research skills, and the critical concerns, including bias,

plagiarism, overreliance, data privacy, and content accuracy. These findings
reinforce the importance of AI literacy for both students and teachers.
         In response to this growing need, several frameworks have been
proposed to conceptualize and assess AI literacy across educational contexts
(Long & Magerko, 2020; Ng et al., 2021; Yi, 2021). Wilton et al. (2022) stress
the need for AI literacy among teachers, citing challenges related to ethical
use, data transparency, and unclear AI functionalities in educational tools.
They advocate for targeted training, interdisciplinary collaboration, and
professional learning communities. Building on this, Velander et al. (2024)
argue that current discourse around AI literacy often prioritizes technical
skills, with less attention given to power dynamics, ethics, and social impact.
         Within the Thai context, national initiatives such as Thailand 4.0
emphasize the development of a skilled workforce and the integration of
technology in education (Wittayasin, 2017). Nevertheless, previous studies
have highlighted challenges in educational quality, workforce preparedness,
and English language proficiency, highlighting the need for targeted reforms
and capacity building (e.g., Buasuwan, 2018; Jones & Pimdee, 2017;
Wittayasin, 2017). For example, Puriwat and Tripopsakul (2020), surveying
132 Thai graduate students nationwide, found the lowest readiness in digital
and information skills, followed by learning and innovation skills, with life
and career skills rated highest. English proficiency, a key requirement for
workforce development, was notably weak. In contrast, Puncreobutr et al.
(2022) reported higher levels of digital literacy among young adults in
Bangkok and surrounding areas. These findings reflect uneven levels of
readiness across different contexts and underscore the need for targeted
interventions aligned with national development strategies.
         Despite growing global interest in AI literacy, research within the Thai
education context remains limited, especially in language teaching and higher
education settings. Existing training initiatives tend to focus on general course
preparation rather than developing specific, targeted skills. Studies
investigating AI literacy in language teaching are scarce (Zhou & Hou, 2025;
Xue, 2025), and those focusing specifically on the English as a Foreign
Language (EFL) context are even more limited (Pan & Wang, 2025), even
though English is widely recognized as a critical component of workforce
development in Thailand.
         This study argues that enhancing AI literacy among Thai EFL
university teachers can improve knowledge transfer and student learning
outcomes. It seeks to address this gap by examining the AI literacy of Thai
EFL university instructors. The findings aim to inform pedagogical practices,
shape policy development, and guide future research within the Thai context,
as well as contribute to broader regional discussions on AI literacy in
education.

                                Literature Review

        The following section reviews relevant literature on AI literacy
frameworks, assessment methods, and research in EFL education with a
particular focus on university teachers, and also provides a broader overview
of the Thai context to capture the overall landscape.

AI Literacy Frameworks

         AI literacy has been conceptualized through various interdisciplinary
frameworks that emphasize knowledge, skills, and critical engagement with
AI technologies. Long and Magerko (2020) define AI literacy as a set of
competencies that enable individuals to critically evaluate, communicate with,
and effectively use AI in everyday contexts. Yi (2021) conceptualizes AI
literacy as an integration of functional, social, and technological literacies,
with an emphasis on metacognition and anticipation.
         Ng et al. (2021), through a systematic review, identify four key
dimensions of AI literacy: knowing and understanding, using and applying,
evaluating and creating, and addressing ethical concerns. Despite providing a
broad conceptual foundation, these frameworks often focus on general users
or student populations
         More recent work has begun to tailor AI literacy frameworks to
educational contexts, with Ma et al. (2024) proposing a six-construct
framework for language education that encompasses benefits, limitations,
prompt design, evaluation, assessment, and ethics. This framework offers a
comprehensive and context-specific approach for examining teachers’
competencies in using generative AI tools in language teaching.

AI Literacy of University Teachers in EFL Contexts

        AI literacy research has largely centered on students, with limited
attention to higher-education teachers. Drawing on the digital literacy of
teachers standard issued by the Ministry of Education of the People’s
Republic of China (2022), Feng and Sumettikoon (2024) developed a
questionnaire covering five dimensions, namely, awareness, knowledge/skills,
application, social responsibility, and professional development, and surveyed
92 EFL teachers from two universities and one vocational college. Teachers
reported high awareness but weaker application, attributed to insufficient
training and institutional support. The authors call for targeted professional
development and collaborative learning structures to translate awareness into
effective practice.


LEARN Journal: Vol. 19, No. 2 (2026)                                      Page 584

Jitpaiboon et al. (2026), pp. 581-605
        A similar pattern is observed in Ma et al. (2024), who introduce a six-
construct framework specifying competencies for the ethical and effective use
of ChatGPT in language education: benefits, limitations, prompt design,
evaluation, assessment, and ethics. Survey responses from 492 educators in
41 countries (university faculty, doctoral students, research staff, and
schoolteachers) showed high literacy regarding benefits but comparatively
low literacy in assessment and prompt design. ChatGPT was used chiefly to
support teaching and learning, especially writing, with concerns centering on
accuracy, limited personalization, and possible reductions in student
motivation and critical thinking. These findings align with Alsaffar (2025),
who highlights the importance of digital readiness for personalized learning.
        Zhou and Hou (2025) explored EFL teachers’ use of AI tools through
interviews with 24 participants. Teachers reported using AI primarily for
assignment distribution, grading, material preparation, translation, and
classroom guidance. They also faced challenges such as limited technical
support and insufficient training. The study highlights the need for
continuous professional development, ethical AI practices, human oversight,
and policy-backed structured training to support effective AI integration.
        Pan and Wang (2025) studied AI literacy among 782 English teachers
from 54 colleges and universities in China, focusing on how age and teaching
experience affect literacy levels. They created and validated a scale with five
components: AI knowledge, use, assessment, design, and ethics. Teachers
were categorized into four literacy profiles: poor, moderate, good, and
excellent. Those aged 27 to 41 and those with four to eleven years of teaching
experience were more likely to exhibit higher levels of AI literacy.
        Xue (2025) examined digital literacy development among nine
Chinese EFL teachers in a university-based professional learning community.
Drawing on data from meetings, interviews, observations, and journals, the
study identified three growth models based on teacher experience. Novice
teachers improved digital skills with mentoring support, veteran teachers
deepened application through experience and reflection, and lead teachers,
already proficient, acted as mentors and role models.

Research on AI Integration in Thai EFL Education

        In Thailand, AI integration in EFL higher education remains
emergent. Ulla et al. (2023) surveyed 17 university EFL teachers with follow-
up interviews and found broadly positive attitudes toward ChatGPT for
lesson planning and activity design, alongside concerns about reliability,
trustworthiness, and student overdependence. Extending this line of inquiry,
Kohnke and Ulla (2024) examined 20 Thai English teachers and reported
early adoption for writing, editing, and planning, but uneven awareness and

Jitpaiboon et al. (2026), pp. 581-605
proficiency; perceived benefits (workload reduction, instructional
enhancement) were tempered by worries about overreliance, reduced
interaction, content accuracy, and academic integrity.
         Complementing these educator-focused studies, Waluyo and
Kusumastuti (2024) examined the experiences of 25 students and 3 teachers
with a range of GenAI tools, including Grammarly, Quillbot, ChatGPT, Bard,
BingChat, and Reverso, reporting high student acceptance and perceived
gains in efficiency and language confidence.
         Several studies have investigated AI implementation within Thai EFL
classrooms, with a strong focus on writing-related contexts. Sawangwan
(2024) found that integrating ChatGPT significantly improved students’
writing skills when paired with teacher guidance, underscoring the importance
of teacher roles in technical, ethical, and instructional support.
Jitpaisarnwattana (2024) used ChatGPT as a diagnostic tool in a paragraph
writing course, demonstrating its effectiveness in delivering structured,
accessible feedback and promoting learner autonomy.
         In more specialized courses, Taylor (2024) explored AI-integrated
blended learning by using tools such as Microsoft Editor, Microsoft Reflect,
and Microsoft Reading Progress in an English for Specific Purposes (ESP)
course for economics students, noting varied experiences based on
proficiency levels and identifying social interaction as the most challenging
aspect. Pucharoen (2024) evaluated an AI-powered speaking coach in a
private university, reporting marked improvements in fluency and
pronunciation, especially in preparing students for careers in customer service
and business.
         Tantivejakul et al. (2024) examined students’ attitudes toward GenAI
in academic and professional PR writing following GenAI tools training,
finding openness to its use in English but hesitancy in professional contexts
due to a lack of clear guidelines and individual differences in readiness.
Likewise, Tangpijaikul (2025) employed ChatGPT in both remedial and
English major classes to provide immediate grammar feedback using simple
prompts like “Check:”, showing its value in supporting lexical and
grammatical awareness through real-time AI-generated feedback.
         These findings suggest that the integration of AI tools in EFL
university classrooms in Thailand remains in its early stages. Preliminary
studies have explored both teacher and student perceptions of generative AI
tools such as ChatGPT and Grammarly, revealing a mix of enthusiasm and
caution. While interest in these technologies is growing, the findings also
highlight a lack of targeted training, inconsistent awareness, and institutional
ambiguity, reflecting a broader global call for more structured and
comprehensive professional development in AI literacy. To date, however,
no study has systematically examined the AI literacy of Thai EFL university

teachers or assessed their competencies across the range of skills needed for
effective, ethical AI integration.
         To address this gap, the present study adopts the six-construct AI
literacy framework developed by Ma et al. (2024), which conceptualizes AI
literacy on a global scale across six key domains: benefits, limitations,
prompts, evaluation, assessment, and ethics. This rigorously validated
framework makes a significant contribution to the field of language teaching
by providing a structured lens through which to evaluate teachers’
competencies, concerns, and patterns of use related to generative AI tools.
Situating this investigation within a national context, the study also broadens
its scope to include AI tools beyond ChatGPT, offering insights relevant to
pedagogical development, institutional policy, and future research.
         Accordingly, this article aims to answer the following research
questions:
         1.    What is the level of AI literacy among Thai EFL university
               teachers?
         2.    In what ways do Thai EFL university teachers use AI tools?
         3.    What challenges do Thai EFL university teachers face when
               using AI tools?

                                   Methodology

Research Design

        This study employed an embedded mixed-methods design,
combining quantitative and qualitative data through questionnaires to
investigate the level of AI literacy and semi-structured group interviews to
gain a deeper understanding of the participants’ views and behaviors.

Participants

        The participants of the study were Thai EFL university teachers
nationwide, including those from both public and private universities,
regardless of age or years of teaching experience. Following the invitation
process, 102 Thai EFL teachers confirmed their participation in the study.
Their demographic information is summarized in Table 1.

         This sample size is comparable to those used in similar studies on AI
literacy and EFL teachers (e.g., Feng & Sumettikoon, 2024; Zhou & Hou,
2025) and is considered sufficient for descriptive statistical analysis and for
capturing diverse perspectives across higher education contexts in Thailand.

Research Instruments

        The questionnaire consisted of three main parts. The first part was
designed to collect demographic information (e.g., gender, age, education,
location, and self-perceived familiarity with AI).
        The second part of the questionnaire adopted the instrument
developed by Ma et al. (2024), which includes 26 items aligned with six
constructs of ChatGPT literacy: benefits, limitations, prompts, evaluation,
assessment, and ethics. Responses were measured on a six-point Likert scale
ranging from 6 (Strongly agree) to 1 (Strongly disagree), consistent with the
original study. Ma et al.’s questionnaire was rigorously validated through item
analysis, reliability analysis, and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA). The
validation yielded strong results, with item-total correlations ranging from
0.619 to 0.876 and Cronbach’s alpha coefficients ranging from 0.82 to 0.94.
The six-construct model also demonstrated good fit in CFA, with CFI =
0.925, TLI = 0.91, RMSEA = 0.07, and SRMR = 0.07. This strong
psychometric support was the primary reason their questionnaire was selected
for use in the current study. To broaden the scope beyond ChatGPT, the
phrase “or other AI tools” was added to relevant items, and the remaining
content was left unchanged.

Jitpaiboon et al. (2026), pp. 581-605
        While the original instrument developed by Ma et al. (2024)
demonstrated high internal consistency, a new reliability analysis was
conducted with the current sample (N = 102), in line with Woodrow’s (2022)
assertion that reliability pertains to the data collected rather than the
instrument itself. According to DeVellis (2016), values above 0.70 are
considered acceptable, with 0.80 or higher preferred (Pallant, 2007).
Cronbach’s alpha coefficients for the six constructs in the current study
ranged from 0.78 to 0.87, indicating acceptable to high internal consistency.
These results suggest that the measurement tool yields reliable, repeatable,
and consistent outcomes, supporting its use with this new sample.
        The third part contained open-ended questions exploring how AI
tools support teaching, the challenges encountered during their use, and the
specific courses and AI tools (other than ChatGPT) involved. The semi-
structured group interview questions were aligned with the questionnaire to
enable data triangulation and to gather more detailed information.

Data Collection

         For the quantitative phase, participants were recruited via email
invitations and posts on social media platforms in Thailand, such as Facebook
and Line. They completed the questionnaire through a Google Form, which
took approximately 20 minutes.
         For the qualitative component, semi-structured group interviews
were conducted via Zoom with ten Thai EFL university teachers. These
participants were purposively selected to ensure representation across
different geographic regions of Thailand and the diverse locations of their
universities. The interviews were conducted in Thai, allowing for ease of
communication and accurate transcription, with participants’ consent.
Participants were organized into small groups of 3-4 to facilitate discussion
and interaction, ensuring that each participant could share their perspectives.
         Before data collection commenced, the research protocol was
submitted to and approved by the Human Research Ethics Committee at the
first author’s institution, with a strong emphasis on voluntary participation
throughout the process.

Data Analysis

       Questionnaire data were primarily analyzed descriptively using SPSS
software to calculate percentages, means (M), and standard deviations (SD).
Open-ended questions and interview data were transcribed and analyzed
thematically through manual content analysis. Data related to the use and

Jitpaiboon et al. (2026), pp. 581-605
challenges of AI tools followed the thematic framework established by Ma et
al. in their data analysis.
         Ma et al. identified themes for AI use in education, including teaching
materials preparation, integration into learning and teaching, formative and
summative assessment, prompt training, feedback on student writing or
language use, revision/proofreading, and use as a self-learning tool. In the
present study, formative and summative assessment were combined into a
single category focused on AI use in assessment and marking. This decision
was made to streamline the analysis and reflect how, in practice, teachers
often do not distinguish sharply between formative and summative functions
when applying AI tools for evaluation purposes.
         Material design was grouped under teaching materials preparation,
and prompt training was excluded because no participants reported engaging
in it. The three instructional phases proposed by Ma et al., namely, Before
Instruction, During Instruction, and After Instruction, were retained. In
addition, an “Across Phases” category was introduced to capture AI uses that
were not confined to a single instructional stage. For AI-related challenges,
the study also adopted Ma et al.’s seven categories: Access, Assessment,
Ethics, Evaluation, Limitations, Prompts, and Teacher Readiness.
         Initial coding was conducted by the first author, and the data were
then divided among the second, third, and fourth authors for independent
review. Interrater reliability was assessed using Krippendorff’s Alpha, yielding
a value of 0.78, which indicates substantial agreement among coders (Landis
& Koch, 1977).

                                       Findings

Question 1: What is the level of AI literacy among Thai EFL university
teachers?

AI literacy levels among Thai EFL university teachers

         According to Table 2, Thai EFL university teachers self-reported a
generally high level of AI literacy (Overall M = 4.67, SD = 1.22) in utilizing
AI tools (including generative AI). These results reflect the teachers’
perceptions and attitudes toward their ability to use AI in educational contexts
rather than measured performance. They showed the strongest confidence in
recognizing AI benefits (M = 5.02, SD = 1.07) and reported a similarly strong
awareness of limitations (M = 4.80, SD = 1.20) and ethical considerations (M
= 4.74, SD = 1.33) related to the use of AI tools. Their self-reported ability
to evaluate AI outputs (M = 4.60, SD = 1.14) and write effective prompts (M
= 4.57, SD = 1.17) is also strong. On the other hand, their average self-
reported use of AI for assessment purposes was somewhat lower (M = 4.26,
SD = 1.38), indicating that the teachers feel less confident about applying AI
tools to assess or evaluate their students’ performance.
         In addition to the mean scores, a large proportion of respondents
selected “agree” or “strongly agree” across most constructs, particularly for
benefits, limitations, and ethics, indicating a generally positive distribution of
AI literacy perceptions.
         The findings indicate that Thai EFL university teachers are well-
informed about various aspects of AI in education, although focused
professional development in AI-based assessment practices could further
strengthen their competencies.

AI literacy among Thai EFL university teachers by familiarity level

         The data analysis confirms that self-perceived familiarity with AI tools
aligns with AI literacy levels among Thai EFL university teachers, as shown
in Table 3. Those who rated themselves as beginners, having used these tools
only once or twice, showed lower literacy scores, and scores increased
significantly with greater experience. The benefits construct, which ranked
second among beginners, rises to the top position at intermediate and expert

Question 2: How do Thai EFL university teachers use AI tools in their
teaching and learning practices?

Content Area

         According to the survey participants, the 190 Thai EFL university
courses where AI tools were integrated into teaching were categorized into
content areas (Table 4). The most frequently mentioned courses were related
to English for Academic Purposes (EAP) or ESP (24%), followed by
speaking (22%) and writing (13%) courses. The fact that courses such as
Artificial Intelligence and Language Learning (included in the “Other”
category) are offered in Thai universities indicates a growing awareness of the
role of AI in Thai EFL tertiary education.

The use of AI tools in EFL university teaching

         All responses (N=102) about the use of AI tools in EFL teaching
were coded and analyzed thematically (see Table 5). The majority of responses
related to the preparation of teaching materials (82%), followed by
revision/proofreading (13%) and integration into learning and teaching
activities (11%). A detailed analysis of each theme is presented below,
organized by frequency and supported by data from semi-structured group
interviews.

        Teaching materials preparation. This theme emerged prominently,
indicated explicitly by terms such as “prepare” and “plan.” Participants
described various uses of AI in preparing teaching resources. For instance,
one respondent stated, “I mainly use AI for preparing course materials,
designing test items, and getting advice for lesson planning.” Another Thai
EFL university teacher mentioned, “I have only used ChatGPT for teaching
preparation-related activities, such as finding additional reading texts tailored
to students’ proficiency levels, creating listening scripts, and designing
exercises.” Two teachers also shared a practical approach during interviews,
explaining that they turn to AI when they lack ideas for classroom activities,
LEARN Journal: Vol. 19, No. 2 (2026)                                               Page 593

Jitpaiboon et al. (2026), pp. 581-605
adapt AI-suggested activities to their teaching contexts, and simplify materials
to align with their students’ competency levels.
         Revision/proofreading. The most frequently mentioned words
related to this theme are “paraphrasing” and “checking grammar.” For
instance, one respondent stated, “I use ChatGPT and other AI tools to get
general ideas, like checking grammar or paraphrasing.” During the interviews,
two teachers echoed these insights, explaining they primarily use AI tools “to
refine writing or paraphrase when struggling to find alternative wording, or
simply to help refine language use.” Another teacher similarly noted, “I often
rely on AI tools to quickly check sentence structure and improve clarity when
preparing materials or reviewing my own writing.” This suggests that AI tools
are also perceived as valuable for ongoing professional development, even
when not fully integrated into classroom practices.
         Integration into learning and teaching activities. This theme
highlights how teachers use AI across classroom contexts, reflecting growing
AI literacy. Several use AI as a writing coach to help students evaluate work,
reflect on feedback, and build real-world communication skills. One teacher
shared, “I generated speeches on AI for listening activities in English for
Hospitality,” whereas another noted, “I allow students to use AI to justify the
readability of texts,” referring to tools like ChatGPT or Grammarly. A similar
approach was noted in translation classes, where AI helped simplify and
clarify texts.
         Teachers also use AI to foster more interactive, student-centered
learning. For instance, one asked students to create different story versions
with AI for group comparison, and another used AI to support idea
generation for class debates. These practices show how AI can promote
collaboration and critical thinking in the classroom.
         Conducting formative and summative assessment. Only a few
Thai EFL university teachers reported using AI tools for evaluating
assignments and supporting grading, as indicated in the open-ended
responses, mainly in writing-related tasks. Terms such as “grading” appeared
occasionally, along with specific references like “assess students’ essays.” For
example, one teacher stated, “ChatGPT is primarily used for lesson planning
and grading, such as assessing student writing assignments.” When asked to
provide more detail during the interview, most teachers mentioned using AI
to help brainstorm test items or quizzes. However, none clearly explained
how AI was used directly in the grading process.
         Self-learning tool/assistant. References to using AI as a self-
learning or professional support tool were limited, possibly due to the study’s
focus on classroom-related practices. Some teachers reported using AI for
personal academic development rather than for direct teaching. For example,
one teacher shared, “I rarely use them for the classroom. I use them for

        Providing feedback on student writing or language use. This
theme was the least frequently observed in the current study. In the survey
responses, one teacher noted, “I use it with lesson planning, developing
teaching materials, and giving feedback,” though no further details were
provided. Despite its low frequency in the survey data, interview responses
provided more detailed insights into how AI tools were used for feedback
purposes. One teacher explained, “I applied ChatGPT with a writing rubric
and asked it to provide feedback on students’ writing. It created a space for
discussion about both the writing pieces and the AI-generated opinions on
the work.”

AI tools used by Thai EFL university teachers

         This section explores AI tools other than ChatGPT. From
participants’ open-ended responses, 146 mentions of AI tools were collected.
As many teachers referred to the same tools, these were consolidated into 38
unique AI tools and categorized by function, as shown in Table 6. Among
the 102 participants, 26 Thai EFL university teachers (25%) reported
experience with ChatGPT only. One teacher mentioned Google Workspace,
which is Google’s suite of cloud-based productivity and collaboration tools
including Gmail, Google Drive, and Google Docs. Since AI features are not
consistently available across all components of Google Workspace, the
response was excluded for being too broad. Nonetheless, the mention of
commonly used tools such as Google Docs and Google Workspace suggests
an emerging awareness of AI integration in everyday digital tools.
         It is noteworthy that respondents who mentioned more than three
different AI tools typically rated themselves at the “advanced level” in AI
familiarity. Several teachers in this category elaborated on their tool usage in
detail. For instance, one teacher stated, “I mostly use Grammarly for grammar
and structure checking during script or essay correction, and ChatGPT and
Gencraft to generate sentences or images for writing prompts.” Another
teacher shared, “Claude AI, ChatGPT, and DeepSeek for academic work;
Perplexity AI for general searching; Copilot and ChatGPT for listening and
speaking activities.”

         Teacher readiness. This emerged as the predominant concern
among Thai EFL university teachers. Issues within this theme included
classroom management difficulties, student engagement, and concerns about
students’ overreliance on AI tools. These concerns reflect teachers’
uncertainty about how to guide students in using AI appropriately, suggesting
a lack of clear strategies or training to support responsible AI use in the
classroom. One participant noted in the open-ended questionnaire,
“Although AI has great potential to enhance students’ writing skills, I am
reluctant to introduce it to my students. Careful pedagogical planning is
needed to integrate AI into classroom lessons.”
         Evaluation. In this construct, concerns regarding accuracy,
relevance, potential bias, and information sources prominently emerged in
the qualitative responses, highlighting persistent uncertainties about the
trustworthiness of AI tools. For instance, one Thai EFL university teacher
commented, “I have not experienced any major challenges. My only concern
is about the trustworthiness of ChatGPT, as I sometimes have to double-
check the information provided by this AI tool.” Another teacher
recommended adopting AI as a “thinking partner,” emphasizing that AI
should facilitate thorough planning rather than dictate actions blindly, a
perspective they suggested should also be encouraged among students.
Insights from the interviews further emphasized these concerns. Teachers
expressed apprehension about validating AI-generated content. For example,
one participant stated, “I am not sure how we can trust or validate the
information generated by GenAI.”
         Ethics. This theme concerns the ethical use of AI and issues related
to plagiarism. One teacher suggested that such concerns can be addressed by
modifying the evaluation approach, specifically, through project-based
assessments that more effectively evaluate students’ competencies and
emphasize the skills demonstrated throughout the process, rather than solely
the final product. Another teacher, during the interview, remarked that this
process-focused approach could help mitigate overreliance on AI, noting,
“Without evaluating the generated sentence, students rely too much on AI
for their writing because they know AI can help them with it.” These insights
highlight the importance of designing assessments that uphold academic
integrity and still leverage the benefits of AI tools in educational settings.
         Limitations. The data revealed several concerns about the
limitations of AI tools, such as usage restrictions in free versions. Some
teachers expressed concerns about the speech generated by AI, describing it
as robotic or unnatural; one commented, “AI cannot focus on specific
consonant sounds like /r/ and /l/ or word stresses if the activity aims to
differentiate the sounds.” Others were worried about reliability issues, with
one teacher noting, “If you want more reliable information from AI, you need

to pay for it, and the costs for one tool are somewhat high.” Additionally,
another teacher explicitly highlighted that “It is true that AI tools are getting
smarter and smarter. Still, they cannot perform all tasks, such as rating video
clips based on very detailed criteria,” emphasizing that despite advancements,
AI still has considerable functional limitations.
         Prompts. Concerns about prompt usage were also notable in the
current study. Most Thai EFL university teachers reported not knowing how
to write effective prompts. They mentioned the need to specify detailed
instructions or provide examples to ensure that the AI understands their
intended request. One teacher noted, “The only challenge is my own prompt
literacy. I am not advanced enough to do the prompting. If I were, I would
have made the best use of ChatGPT.” Another piece of evidence pointed out
that “Prompts are crucial input in collaborating with AI tools; the outcomes
would be incompatible if we do not place precise and effective prompts.”
         Access. Seven out of eleven comments regarding access to AI tools
raised concerns about cost. Thai EFL university teachers noted that paid
subscriptions tend to offer more reliable and higher-quality features than free
versions, which limits access for those unable to afford them. As one teacher
explained during an interview, “The limitation drawn from using AI tools is
restricted access to their full functions due to the requirement of paid
subscriptions.”
         The remaining comments addressed broader access challenges
beyond cost. These included unclear policies regarding the extent to which
AI is permitted in educational settings, unequal access to devices, and
unstable internet connections that hinder effective use of AI tools.
         Assessment. Only a few Thai EFL university teachers commented
on assessment-related issues. One teacher remarked, “It is difficult to evaluate
students’ performance if they are allowed to use AI tools during exams.” The
overall lack of discussion may suggest that this area is being overlooked,
possibly due to limited literacy in applying AI tools for assessment purposes.

                                       Discussions

         The findings provide valuable insights into the AI literacy levels of
Thai EFL university teachers. Participants reported AI literacy scores across
all six constructs ranging from 4.26 to 5.02, with an overall mean of 4.67.
These results demonstrate consistently high levels of AI literacy and slightly
higher scores than those reported by language teachers across 41 countries in
Ma et al. (2024), whose scores ranged from 3.95 to 4.70 with an overall mean
of 4.59.
         Thai EFL university teachers rated themselves highest in the
“Benefits” construct and lowest in “Assessment,” reflecting a pattern also

observed in the findings of Ma et al. (2024). This alignment suggests a shared
recognition of AI’s educational potential, alongside a common need for
greater support in assessment practices. The similarity in results, despite
involving a different group of participants, also supports the validity of Ma et
al.’s six-construct framework.
          These findings are consistent with prior research highlighting positive
awareness of AI tools in the Thai EFL context. For example, Puncreobutr et
al. (2022) emphasized the general digital literacy of Thai people, with studies
by Ulla et al. (2023) and Kohnke and Ulla (2024) reporting encouraging
attitudes towards AI in language teaching, particularly among Thai EFL
university instructors. Despite this, the integration of AI in assessment
remains underdeveloped. A closely related study by Jitpaisarnwattana (2024)
explored the use of ChatGPT for diagnostic assessment and feedback
generation, but without incorporating evaluative grading. This points to a
need for further exploration into AI’s role in comprehensive assessment
practices.
          The consistently low mean scores in the “Assessment” construct,
even among teachers who identified themselves as being at an “advanced”
level of AI familiarity, align with the findings of Feng and Sumettikoon
(2024). While digital awareness may be high, it does not always translate into
effective digital application. This limitation may also be influenced by broader
factors, including uncertainty about ethical boundaries in AI-assisted grading,
limited assessment literacy related to AI tools, and institutional constraints
such as unclear policies and lack of standardized guidelines for AI use in
evaluation.
          Self-reported familiarity was closely associated with usage frequency:
more frequent users reported higher AI literacy, echoing Kohnke and Ulla’s
(2024) observation that some teachers had only minimal exposure (e.g., a
single trial). Across proficiency levels, assessment remained the weakest
competence, underscoring the need for targeted professional development.
“Advanced” users typically employed multiple tools beyond ChatGPT and
described purpose-specific applications. With adequate institutional support,
these digitally skilled teachers can serve as lead educators and mentors (Xue,
2025). As such, institutional backing, including funded tool subscriptions and
infrastructure, is essential (Ngelambong et al., 2025).
          One of the key findings is that AI tools were most frequently
integrated into EAP and ESP courses (24%). This pattern aligns with an
expanding body of Thai-based research on AI use in these instructional
contexts. For instance, Taylor (2024) explored AI-supported learning in
English for Economics, Pucharoen (2024) examined its integration within the
School of Entrepreneurial Management, and Tantivejakul et al. (2024)
investigated student attitudes toward generative AI in academic and

professional public relations writing. Collectively, these studies underscore
the role of AI in enhancing students’ career-oriented communication skills.
The introduction of courses such as Artificial Intelligence and Language
Learning further reflects growing institutional awareness of AI’s role in Thai
EFL tertiary education.
          In terms of practical application, the study found that Thai EFL
university teachers primarily used AI for preparing teaching materials. This
differs from findings reported by Ma et al. (2024), who noted that AI
integration was most common in general teaching activities, and Zhou and
Hou (2025), who found that AI tools were frequently used for assignment
distribution and grading. Kohnke and Ulla (2024) pointed out that, in the
Thai context, centrally developed lesson plans and teaching materials may
limit individual teachers’ autonomy in adopting AI tools more broadly.
Furthermore, uncertainty regarding institutional policies, particularly
concerning the extent to which AI is allowed in classroom settings, may also
act as a barrier to full integration.
          A particularly important pedagogical insight emerging from these
findings is the concept of AI as a “thinking partner,” where teachers and
students use AI to support idea development, reflection, and critical
evaluation rather than relying on it as an authoritative source. This perspective
extends existing discussions of AI use in language education by emphasizing
its role in fostering critical engagement rather than passive reliance.
          The results also highlight the need for context-specific professional
training that goes beyond general AI awareness and focuses on pedagogical
applications. Training programs should include practical strategies for
evaluating AI-generated outputs, designing AI-assisted assessment tasks, and
developing prompt literacy. In addition, institutions should provide clearer
guidelines and support structures to help teachers integrate AI tools
responsibly and effectively into their teaching.

                                   Conclusions

        The findings of this study show that Thai EFL university teachers are
aware of the benefits of AI tools in language teaching, yet also revealing key
areas of weakness in their application. These results point to the need for
targeted support to address teachers’ instructional needs in response to the
growing demand for professional development in the AI era. They also
underscore the importance of integrating AI literacy into English language
instruction to better prepare students for a technology-driven society.
        Human involvement remains essential in AI-supported education to
ensure accuracy, ethical use, and sound pedagogy. Teachers and students need
to engage critically with AI-generated content and use it responsibly.

Effective integration depends not only on ongoing professional development
and policy support, but also on teachers’ ability to adapt their pedagogical
practices. As classrooms evolve, developing new literacies, including an
understanding of AI’s limitations and ethical implications, becomes
increasingly important. Despite rapid technological change, human
interaction remains central, with teachers continuing to play a key role in
facilitating meaningful learning. These findings align with prior studies (e.g.,
Kasneci et al., 2023; Kohnke & Ulla, 2024; Zhou & Hou, 2025).
          Future research could explore underrepresented educational contexts,
as well as institutional and cultural differences, to support more inclusive and
effective AI practices in language education. Further work is needed to
examine AI’s role in assessment and feedback across both local and
international settings, especially in relation to challenges such as limited
teacher capacity and students’ overreliance on AI tools. Examining AI
through the lens of power dynamics, as suggested by Velander et al. (2024),
may also offer deeper insight into its broader implications in educational
discourse.
          In terms of practical implications, teacher training programs could
include workshops on AI-assisted assessment design, prompt engineering for
educational tasks, and strategies for critically evaluating AI-generated content.
At the institutional level, universities should consider developing clear
guidelines on AI use in teaching and assessment, providing access to reliable
AI tools, and supporting communities of practice where teachers can share
experiences and best practices.
          This study contributes to addressing the gap in AI literacy research
within the Thai EFL context, where such surveys remain limited. The findings
are constrained by the framework used and the timing of data collection.
Although the study involved a relatively large sample of Thai EFL teachers,
future research with broader samples may yield different insights.

Jenjira Jitpaiboon: An assistant professor at King Mongkut’s Institute of
